data_schema.title: USDA Directive Extraction Schema v2.1 (DR/DM)
data_schema.description: Extracts metadata and structured policy statements from 3000 series USDA Departmental Regulation (DR) or Departmental Manual (DM). Governing rules: (1) Any field described as verbatim must be copied character-for-character from the source document. Never paraphrase, merge, abbreviate, summarize, or insert ellipses. (2) Do not infer. If the source does not support an optional field, leave the field out entirely. Never return an empty string or a guess. (3) Only the label fields in policy_statements (statement_kind, statement_function, modal_use, normative_force, actor_basis) are interpretations. Every other field is quoted or copied from the document.

document_type.description: Type of document as printed in the header, such as 'Departmental Regulation' or 'Departmental Manual'.

issuing_organization.description: Organization issuing the document, verbatim from the header.

issuing_location.description: Location of the issuing organization, verbatim from the header.

regulation_number.description: Official document number from the header, verbatim, for example 'DR 3105-001'.

subject.description: Subject or title of the document, verbatim from the header.

issue_date.description: Issue date from the header, as written.

expiration_date.description: Expiration date from the header, as written. Leave out if none is printed.

opi.description: Office of Primary Interest (OPI) from the header, verbatim.

supersedes.description: The prior document this document supersedes. Take all values from the supersession paragraph in the body (usually under Special Instructions/Cancellations), NOT from the header. Leave the whole object out if the document supersedes nothing.

document_number.description: Number of the superseded document as written in the supersession paragraph. If it is identical to this document's own number, still copy it from the supersession paragraph, not the header.

document_title.description: Title of the superseded document as written in the supersession paragraph.

document_date.description: Date of the superseded document as written in the supersession paragraph.

scope.description: The text of the Scope section, verbatim. Do not add words. Leave out if the document has no Scope section.

purpose.description: The text of the Purpose section, verbatim. Do not add words. Leave out if the document has no Purpose section.

inquiries.description: Contact information from the Inquiries section. Leave out any property the document does not state; never return an empty string.

office.description: Office or division named for inquiries, verbatim. Leave out if the document names no office.

email.description: Email address given for inquiries, verbatim, without trailing punctuation. Leave out if none is given.

table_of_contents.description: Top-level entries of the printed table of contents, in order, including appendices. Return an empty list if the document prints no table of contents.

section_number.description: Section or appendix identifier as printed, for example '1.' or 'Appendix A'.

section_title.description: Section or appendix title as printed in the table of contents.

page.description: Page number exactly as printed in the table of contents, for example '2' or 'A-1'. Copy it even if the section actually starts on a different page. Leave out if no page number is printed.

actors.description: Registry of every distinct entity that the policy text names in an acting role. One entry per entity. Include every entity used as actor_name in policy_statements. Also include entities the document names in a role without being directed to act (mark those mentioned_only). Documents (bylaws, regulations, directives) are NEVER actors and must not appear here. Return an empty list if the document names no actors.

name.description: The entity's name exactly as written in the policy text, without a leading article ('the') and without a possessive. Keep a compound name intact if the document writes it as one phrase, for example 'USDA Mission Areas, agencies, and staff offices'. This is the join key used by actor_name in policy_statements, so spell it identically there.

components.description: ONLY for a name that joins separate entities with commas or 'and' (for example 'USDA Mission Areas, agencies, and staff offices' gives 'USDA Mission Areas', 'agencies', 'staff offices'). NEVER split a job title from the organization that qualifies it ('Director of IT, Office of the Inspector General' is ONE position), and never split an organization name from the position it modifies ('Office of the Chief Information Officer (OCIO) Associate CIOs (ACIO)' is ONE group). Each component is a verbatim substring of the name. Leave out for single entities.

items.description: One verbatim component of a compound actor name.

actor_type.description: Kind of entity. Use exactly one of: position (a job title, singular or plural, for example 'USDA CIO' or 'Mission Area Assistant CIOs'), office (an organizational unit, for example 'OCIO Executive Secretariat'), council_or_body (a council, committee, board, or similar body), group (a category of organizations or units, not job titles, for example 'USDA Mission Areas, agencies, and staff offices'), external_entity (an entity outside the document's authority), program_or_system (an IT initiative, system, program, or project that the document says must act or conform).

binding_status.description: bound_by_this_document: the document directs, permits, or assigns a function or role to this entity and has authority over it. mentioned_only: the document names the entity but cannot or does not impose anything on it (for example a council or agency outside USDA that the document says a USDA body partners with).

policy_statements.description: Structured statements from the numbered body sections only (not the table of contents, not the appendices). RULES. (a) SENTENCES: emit one statement per sentence. If a paragraph has more than one sentence, give each its own statement with ids suffixed .s1, .s2, and so on. Abbreviations and legal citations ('U.S.C.', 'CFR', '§', 'et seq.') do not end a sentence. (b) LISTS: when text introduces a list (usually ends with a colon, for example 'The USDA CIO will:'), emit the introducing text as one statement with statement_kind 'lead_in', and emit EVERY item of the list as its own statement with statement_kind 'list_item' and parent_statement_id set to the id of the lead_in. Never skip list items, including lists of legal authorities. For a list inside a list, parent_statement_id is the immediate parent. (c) NEVER merge text from different sentences, paragraphs, or list items into one statement. (d) Copy text exactly; do not summarize. (e) PRONOUNS: when a sentence's subject is a pronoun ('It', 'Its', 'They') that refers to a named actor in the preceding sentence, resolve it: set actor_name to that actor and actor_basis to resolved_from_prior_sentence. (f) DOCUMENT AS SUBJECT: when the grammatical subject is the document itself ('This DR', 'This policy', 'Nothing in this DR'), leave actor_name out; the entities the document acts on belong in target.

statement_id.description: Printed numbering path of the statement: section number, then paragraph letter, then item number in parentheses, for example '1', '3.a', '5.d.s2', '6.a(1)'. Add '.sN' only when a paragraph contains more than one sentence. Must be unique within the document.

statement_kind.description: standalone: a complete sentence that stands on its own. lead_in: text that introduces a list and is incomplete without its items. list_item: a list item that completes its lead_in.

parent_statement_id.description: Include ONLY when statement_kind is list_item: the statement_id of its immediate lead_in. For every other statement leave this field out entirely; never return an empty string.

section_number.description: Number of the section containing the statement, digits only, for example '6'.

section_title.description: Title of the section containing the statement, as shown in the table of contents, for example 'Roles and Responsibilities'.

source_text.description: VERBATIM text of this one sentence or list item exactly as printed, including trailing punctuation such as ':' or ';' and including any list-ending words such as 'and'. No paraphrase, no ellipses, no text from any other statement. For a list_item, give only the item's own text, not the lead_in.

statement_function.description: What the statement does. obligation: a required action or compliance requirement on an actor. responsibility: a standing duty or function assigned to an actor, including present-tense descriptions of what a body does. role_designation: assigns an entity to a role, for example membership or voting status. authority: names a legal source of authority or a grant of authority. scope: states what or whom the document applies to. purpose: states why the document or a body exists. definition: defines a term. condition: states a standalone triggering condition. exception: carves out an exception. savings_clause: states that the document does not displace existing authorities or delegations. effectivity: states when the document takes effect or how long it lasts. supersession: states that the document replaces another. classification_rule: states a rule that classifies something or applies a requirement when a status is met. reference: points to another document or location. inquiry: tells who may be contacted. container: use for every lead_in statement. other: none of the above.

modal_verb.description: The modal word or phrase of the statement's MAIN clause, exactly as written, for example 'will', 'can', 'may', 'must', 'shall', 'must not'. Ignore modals inside relative or subordinate clauses (for 'advises the USDA CIO on IT matters that may become IT investments', the 'may' is not the statement's modal). For a list_item whose own text has no modal, copy the modal from its lead_in. Leave out if the main clause has no modal.

modal_use.description: deontic: the main-clause modal directs, permits, or prohibits action by an actor (for example 'The Deputy CIO will serve', 'can direct questions'). predictive: the modal only states what will happen or remain true (for example 'It will remain in effect until superseded'). none: the main clause has no modal.

normative_force.description: mandatory: deontic 'will', 'shall', or 'must' directing an actor to act or to serve in a role. prohibitive: deontic 'must not', 'shall not', or 'may not'. permissive: deontic 'may' or 'can'. assigned: a present-tense statement with no deontic modal that assigns or describes a function, duty, or role of a named actor (for example 'The CIO Council advises the USDA CIO on...', 'It assesses the needs of...'); use it only when actor_name is present, and never for purpose statements. descriptive: everything else with no deontic force, including purpose, scope, supersession, effectivity, savings clauses, references, authorities, definitions, and statements about the document itself or about other documents. not_applicable: use for every lead_in; its force is carried by its list_items.

actor_name.description: The entity directed to act, permitted to act, or assigned a function or role by this statement, spelled exactly as in the matching actors[].name. It must appear in source_text or in the lead_in's text (leading article removed); for a resolved pronoun, copy it from the antecedent sentence. Leave out when the statement binds no actor: scope, supersession, effectivity, savings clauses, statements about documents (including bylaws), and any statement whose subject is the document itself ('This DR', 'This policy', 'Nothing in this DR'). Never supply an actor that is not stated in the text or resolvable from the preceding sentence. Always leave out for lead_in statements.

actor_basis.description: Include ONLY when actor_name is present; otherwise leave this field out entirely. explicit_in_statement: the actor appears in this statement's own source_text. inherited_from_lead_in: the actor appears only in the lead_in that this list_item completes. resolved_from_prior_sentence: the subject is a pronoun resolved to the actor named in the preceding sentence.

target.description: VERBATIM phrase naming what the action is directed at or what the statement applies to, starting at the first word after any leading article ('a', 'an', 'the'). For a role_designation, the body or unit the role is within (for example 'CIO Council'). Leave out if none.

resulting_status.description: VERBATIM phrase naming the status or role that a role_designation or classification_rule confers, for example 'voting member' or 'advisory (non-voting) members'. Leave out for other statements.

conditions.description: VERBATIM phrases that restrict when or to what the statement applies, for example 'that the CIO Council designates as enterprise initiatives'. Do NOT treat a non-restrictive descriptive phrase set off by commas (for example 'appointed by the USDA CIO' in 'The Secretariat, appointed by the USDA CIO, will serve') as a condition. Leave out if there are none.

items.description: One verbatim condition phrase copied from source_text.

cross_references.description: Other documents, laws, or regulations cited in source_text, each copied verbatim as ONE entry per cited authority, including its code citation (for example 'The Clinger-Cohen Act of 1996, 40 United States Code (U.S.C.) § 11101 et seq.' is one entry; for a list_item that is just a citation, the entry is the item text without the trailing ';' or 'and'). Never add a separate entry for a title that is part of the same citation (the words 'Chief Information Officer' after '7 CFR § 2.32'). Never list generic categories such as 'law' or 'Federal regulation'. Leave out if none.

acronyms.description: Acronyms and abbreviations listed in the acronym appendix, one entry per row, in order. Return an empty list if the document has no acronym appendix.

acronym.description: Acronym or abbreviation exactly as printed.

authorities_and_references.description: Entries of the Authorities and References appendix, one per entry, each copied verbatim, including any date, in order. Return an empty list if the document has no such appendix.

items.description: One appendix entry exactly as printed, joined across line breaks.

policy_statements.source_text: This Departmental Regulation (DR) establishes the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) policy for configuration management, security configuration management (SecCM), which is also known as secure or security-focused configuration management, and inventory management.
policy_statements.target: United States Department of Agriculture (USDA) policy for configuration management, security configuration management (SecCM), which is also known as secure or security-focused configuration management, and inventory management

policy_statements.source_text: In addition to configuration management, SecCM, and inventory management, this policy addresses prohibitions or restrictions on functions, services, ports, protocols, and software installation and usage, based on the configuration management (CM) controls in the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Special Publication (SP 800-53 Revision 4, Security and Privacy Controls for Federal Information Systems and Organizations.
cross_references: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Special Publication (SP 800-53 Revision 4, Security and Privacy Controls for Federal Information Systems and Organizations
policy_statements.target: prohibitions or restrictions on functions, services, ports, protocols, and software installation and usage

policy_statements.source_text: These restrictions and prohibitions are necessary to prevent unauthorized connection of devices, unauthorized tunneling, and unauthorized transfer of information that violates copyright laws or affords access to or use of unauthorized or illegal materials.

It is the policy of USDA to comply with Federal laws, regulations, and standards to establish, implement, and enforce a configuration management policy to continually manage risks to USDA information resources.

This policy complies with the requirements of the Federal Information Security Modernization Act of 2014 (FISMA), 44 United States Code (U.S.C.) § 3551; Federal Information Processing Standards Publication (FIPS PUB) 200, Minimum Security Requirements for Federal Information and Information Systems; NIST SP 800-53 Revision 4; NIST SP 800-128, Guide for Security-Focused Configuration Management of Information Systems; and other Federal laws, regulations, requirements, and standards regarding configuration management.
cross_references: Federal Information Security Modernization Act of 2014 (FISMA), 44 United States Code (U.S.C.) § 3551
Federal Information Processing Standards Publication (FIPS PUB) 200, Minimum Security Requirements for Federal Information and Information Systems
NIST SP 800-128, Guide for Security-Focused Configuration Management of Information Systems

This policy addresses monitoring for actual or potential security violations and enforcing compliance to scan for, prevent access to, or use of unauthorized software applications.
It also addresses secure configurations and integrating security considerations into configuration management processes.
Complementary policies include:
DR 3160-001, Licensed Information Technology (IT) Software;

DR 3180-001, Information Technology Standards;

The term “agencies” or “USDA agencies” will be assumed to generically refer to Mission Areas, agencies, and staff offices unless otherwise specified.

policy_statements.source_text: The term “USDA employee” means a Federal civil servant employed by, detailed or assigned to, USDA, including members of the Armed Forces.
The term “USDA personnel” means USDA employees, contractors, affiliates, interns, fellows, and volunteers who work for, or on behalf of, USDA, and whose work is overseen by USDA employees.
The terms “hardware” and “hardware asset” are used in this policy in conformance with Federal guidance for FY 2018 CIO FISMA Metrics Version 1.0.
A related term is “hardware component.”
Examples are:
Endpoint devices such as servers, workstations, and laptops;
Mobile devices, such as smartphones and tablets;
Networking devices such as routers, switches, firewalls, wireless access points, intrusion detection/intrusion prevention systems, modems, and network address translators;
Other communication devices such as alarms, physical access control devices, and virtual private networks (VPN);

Network-addressable input and output devices such as printers, copiers, scanners, network accessible storage devices, Voice over Internet Protocol (VoIP) phones, and other network-addressable devices; and
Virtual machines that can be addressed as if they are a separate physical machine.

The term “material conflict of interest” means a conflict of interest is considered ‘material’ if a reasonable disinterested person would take it into account in exercising judgment or making a decision.

The terms “software,” “software asset,” and “software component” are used in this policy to encompass types of software such as commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) and open-source software including applications, code snippets, and code libraries; operating systems, databases, functional applications, middleware; security-relevant software such as antivirus; custom-developed software; firmware; and software code incorporated by vendors into hardware appliances to perform tasks such as big data analytics or intrusion protection.
“Firmware” may be mentioned separately from “software.”
The term “vulnerability” is used instead of “flaw” to describe weaknesses in systems or protection mechanisms that must be remediated.
Configuration management encompasses the planning and processes to manage the impacts of changes or differences on an information system or network and, by extension, on an organization.

Configuration management promotes the security objectives of confidentiality, integrity, and availability for information systems and ensures that the state of the hardware, software, communications services, documentation, and other artifacts (all formally referred to as “configuration items”) for a system can be accurately determined at any time.

Furthermore, properly managing the inventory of hardware and software assets and the configurations of those assets is an essential factor in monitoring the status of security controls, identifying potential security-related problems in information systems, and reducing the risk of exploitation or inadvertent failures.

Configuration management practices support information security continuous monitoring, which is described in NIST SP 800-137, Information Security Continuous Monitoring (ISCM) for Federal Information Systems and Organizations.
cross_references: NIST SP 800-137, Information Security Continuous Monitoring (ISCM) for Federal Information Systems and Organizations

policy_statements.source_text: ISCM provides an up-to-date view of information security risks.
policy_statements.target: up-to-date view of information security risks

policy_statements.source_text: For example, outputs of ISCM include security-related information pertaining to the accuracy of the information system component inventory, which in turn is needed for managing remediation of configuration and patch vulnerabilities, reporting metrics to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), and ongoing authorization of the system.
Understanding the evolving nature of vulnerabilities as they appear in a system can help security managers and system owners to direct appropriate changes.
Changes to IT products (hardware and software) include installation or implementation, modification or patching, and deletion or uninstalling.
Changes to system-related documentation such as administrator guides, diagrams, and system security plans are also subject to configuration management controls.
Configuration management planning and procedures provide a repeatable mechanism for implementing system modifications in a controlled environment.
This allows the established configuration management process to be conducted throughout the lifecycle of the system.
The system lifecycle begins with establishing an initial baseline for all information system components, with subsequent updates to the baseline as controlled changes are implemented.
Configuration change control procedures identify the steps required to ensure that all changes are properly requested, evaluated for both functional and security impacts, and authorized.
Configuration management also requires procedures for identifying, recording, evaluating, tracking, coordinating, reporting, and controlling configuration items.
General objectives of configuration management are to:
Provide controls to ensure that the information system operates correctly throughout its life;
Maintain a current, accurate inventory of the information system and associated documentation as the system changes;
Ensure that the configurations of all information system components are approved, available to those with a need-to-know, current, complete, and accurate at all times;

Ensure that the pertinent physical (functional) and logical (virtual) interfaces among systems, equipment, and software are correctly and adequately documented in the System Security Plans (SSP), Interconnection Security Agreements (ISA), and Information System Contingency Plans;
Promote hardware and software maintenance efficiency by ensuring that change proposals are appropriately acted upon; and
Ensure that the impact of any change to system functionality, security, privacy, performance, or cost is known at the time the change is approved.
SecCM activities include:
Identification and recording of configurations that impact the security posture of the information system, privacy information, and the organization;
Consideration of security risks in approving the initial configuration;
Analysis of security implications of changes to the information system configuration; and
Documentation of the approved and implemented changes.

Inventory scans, also referred to as discovery scans, probe wired or wireless networks, identifying hardware and software assets for inventory purposes, open ports and services running on those ports, and protocols.
Vulnerability scans assess compliance with technical security controls, such as identifying configuration issues, missing or out-of-date patches, or other vulnerabilities.
Configuration management procedures govern remediation of those vulnerabilities.
Some hardware assets, such as network equipment, printers, application appliances, and mainframes, may not support endpoint agents.
For these, a different tool must be used to perform agentless scanning.
policy_statements.target: agentless scanning

policy_statements.source_text: These devices are sometimes termed “non-managed” or “unmanaged” assets, which means an installed agent does not actively manage them, but they still require oversight through other technical or non-technical means.
Unmanaged assets must adhere to configuration management procedures.

policy_statements.source_text: Requirements for configuration management, SecCM, and use of mandatory secure configurations will be included in all statements of work and procurement requests for all contracts involving acquisition of:
Hardware and software assets; and
Services for integration, development, maintenance of information systems, software, or hardware components.
USDA agencies will establish, implement, and maintain procedures for configuration management, SecCM, inventory management, and change control processes to include:
Robust integration throughout the lifecycle activities of all information systems and services used or operated by, for, or on behalf of USDA;

Tight integration with vulnerability management processes such as software vulnerability remediation, application of security-relevant software updates (e.g., patches, service packs, hot fixes, anti-malware signatures), and system configuration and hardening;

Integration with other processes such as risk assessment and risk management, plans of action and milestones (POA&M), security assessments, continuous monitoring, incident management, and system error handling;
Management of the inventory of hardware and software assets (components or configuration items) and system documentation;
Identifying and reporting high-value assets (HVA), at least annually, to the Information Security Center (ISC) via email to ASOC.Outreach@usda.gov and cyber.incidents@usda.gov;
conditions: at least annually

policy_statements.source_text: Identification of secure configurations to be applied;
Monitoring activities (such as through automated scans) to ensure current, complete, and accurate configuration baselines and to detect unauthorized or undocumented changes; and
Developing and reporting metrics for compliance with policy and procedures.
Configuration change control procedures and processes will address:
Scheduled changes and upgrades such as modifications to, or removal of, hardware or software components, changes to configuration settings, and opening or closing of ports;
Emergency and time-sensitive changes;
Automated change mechanisms such as patch installations or updates to malicious code protection; and
Unauthorized or undocumented changes that have been discovered, including managing these as vulnerabilities or incidents.
Mission Area, agency, and staff office policies (if they exist) and procedures will address processes and any required documentation for:
Proposing and justifying changes;
Reviewing proposed changes and evaluating security, privacy, functional, and other impacts of proposed changes;
Meeting timeframe standards for security-relevant changes based on criteria, such as:
The severity of the vulnerability and compliance with policy and procedures for scanning and remediation of configuration and patch vulnerabilities;
The security categorization of the information system; and
Releases from vendors of malicious code protection mechanisms.
Determining whether a given change or set of changes constitute an acceptable security risk and documentation of the risk-based decision along with requirements for controls to mitigate the risk;
Handling exception requests, such as deviations from required secure configurations and settings, to include the criteria for approving or denying the requests and documenting the decisions;

Determining the degree and type of testing needed for specific types of changes (e.g., no testing of anti-malware signatures; validating vulnerability remediation; or a full security assessment on a mission-critical system), privacy impact for individual privacy, and for the security impact level of the system (e.g., a separate test environment for high-impact systems);
Approving, denying, or deferring proposed changes;
Implementing approved changes and verifying the change was implemented correctly;
Ensuring that supporting and related documentation such as design documents, component inventories, security plans, and POA&Ms are also updated;
Closing change requests; and
Retaining and archiving baselines.
The configuration change control processes will be overseen by a duly established configuration control board (CCB) consisting of USDA personnel who:
Are qualified to control and approve proposed changes; and
Do not have a material conflict of interest regarding approving proposed changes.

Authority or ability to make changes to information systems, baseline configurations, and the inventory will be limited to qualified, duly authorized USDA personnel through appropriate access control mechanisms.
policy_statements.target: qualified, duly authorized USDA personnel

policy_statements.source_text: USDA agencies will support the maintenance of the Departmentwide inventory of information systems and information system components by documenting all data elements required by the Department in support of reporting and other activities as follows:
For managed components (those with installed agents), identify, correct, or add components that have incorrect or missing values for the Agency Identification number and Computer Group fields; and
conditions: For managed components (those with installed agents)

policy_statements.source_text: For non-managed components (those without installed agents), maintain a current inventory that includes manually tracked information such as the system name, property number, serial number, contact information for the responsible system owner and system administrator, and physical location information and information collected through an inventory scan.
conditions: For non-managed components (those without installed agents)

policy_statements.source_text: USDA agencies will develop, document, and maintain a current, complete, and accurate inventory and baseline configuration of each information system or service and its components under configuration control and:
Contain no duplicates, ensuring that each component in the inventory falls within the accreditation boundary of only one information system;
Track all assets throughout their lifecycle from acquisition and installation through retirement and removal;

Configuration management encompasses the planning and processes to manage the impacts of changes or differences on an information system or network and, by extension, on an organization.

Configuration management promotes the security objectives of confidentiality, integrity, and availability for information systems and ensures that the state of the hardware, software, communications services, documentation, and other artifacts (all formally referred to as “configuration items”) for a system can be accurately determined at any time.

Furthermore, properly managing the inventory of hardware and software assets and the configurations of those assets is an essential factor in monitoring the status of security controls, identifying potential security-related problems in information systems, and reducing the risk of exploitation or inadvertent failures.

Configuration management practices support information security continuous monitoring, which is described in NIST  SP 800-137 , *Information Security Continuous Monitoring (ISCM) for Federal Information Systems and Organizations*. ISCM provides an up-to-date view of information security risks. For example, outputs of ISCM include security-related information pertaining to the accuracy of the information system component inventory, which in turn is needed for managing remediation of configuration and patch vulnerabilities, reporting metrics to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB), and ongoing authorization of the system.

Changes to IT products (hardware and software) include installation or implementation, modification or patching, and deletion or uninstalling.
Changes to system-related documentation such as administrator guides, diagrams, and system security plans are also subject to configuration management controls.
Configuration management planning and procedures provide a repeatable mechanism for implementing system modifications in a controlled environment.
This allows the established configuration management process to be conducted throughout the lifecycle of the system.
The system lifecycle begins with establishing an initial baseline for all information system components, with subsequent updates to the baseline as controlled changes are implemented.
Configuration change control procedures identify the steps required to ensure that all changes are properly requested, evaluated for both functional and security impacts, and authorized.
Configuration management also requires procedures for identifying, recording, evaluating, tracking, coordinating, reporting, and controlling configuration items.
General objectives of configuration management are to:
Provide controls to ensure that the information system operates correctly throughout its life;
Maintain a current, accurate inventory of the information system and associated documentation as the system changes;
Ensure that the configurations of all information system components are approved, available to those with a need-to-know, current, complete, and accurate at all times;

Ensure that the pertinent physical (functional) and logical (virtual) interfaces among systems, equipment, and software are correctly and adequately documented in the System Security Plans (SSP), Interconnection Security Agreements (ISA), and Information System Contingency Plans;
Promote hardware and software maintenance efficiency by ensuring that change proposals are appropriately acted upon; and
Ensure that the impact of any change to system functionality, security, privacy, performance, or cost is known at the time the change is approved.
Identification and recording of configurations that impact the security posture of the information system, privacy information, and the organization;
Consideration of security risks in approving the initial configuration;
Analysis of security implications of changes to the information system configuration; and
Documentation of the approved and implemented changes.
